questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: What do all waves transfer?
questions.hint: Think about the wave going past a bobbing duck — the duck doesn't travel with it.
questions.explanation: All waves transfer energy from one place to another without transferring matter. The particles of the medium oscillate but don't travel with the wave.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Science KM, Unit 3 Waves, Light and Sound

further_learning.title: Sound, Light and Vision – Oak National Academy

questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: Which is the distance between two neighbouring peaks of a wave?
questions.hint: The 'length' of one full wave.
questions.explanation: Wavelength is the distance from one peak (or trough) to the next. It's measured in metres and given the symbol λ (lambda).
questions.source: CHS Y8 Science KM, Unit 3 Waves, Light and Sound

further_learning.title: Sound, Light and Vision – Oak National Academy

questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: What does the amplitude of a wave represent?
options: How loud or bright the wave is (energy)
How many waves pass per second
questions.answer: How loud or bright the wave is (energy)
questions.hint: Bigger amplitude = more energy.
questions.explanation: Amplitude is the maximum height of a peak from the midline. Bigger amplitude means more energy — louder sound, brighter light.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Science KM, Unit 3 Waves, Light and Sound

further_learning.title: Sound, Light and Vision – Oak National Academy

questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: What is frequency measured in?
questions.hint: Named after the scientist Heinrich Hertz.
questions.explanation: Frequency is the number of waves passing a point per second. Its unit is the hertz (Hz). 1 Hz = 1 wave per second.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Science KM, Unit 3 Waves, Light and Sound

further_learning.title: Sound, Light and Vision – Oak National Academy

questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: What is the key difference between transverse and longitudinal waves?
options: Transverse vibrate at right angles to direction of travel; longitudinal vibrate along it
questions.answer: Transverse vibrate at right angles to direction of travel; longitudinal vibrate along it
questions.hint: Think slinky shaken side-to-side (transverse) vs pushed back-and-forth (longitudinal).
questions.explanation: Transverse waves (light, water ripples) have oscillations perpendicular to the direction of energy travel. Longitudinal waves (sound) have oscillations along the direction of travel — compressions and rarefactions.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Science KM, Unit 3 Waves, Light and Sound

further_learning.title: Sound, Light and Vision – Oak National Academy

questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: Sound waves are an example of which type of wave?
questions.hint: Air particles vibrate back and forth in the same direction as the sound travels.
questions.explanation: Sound is a longitudinal wave. Air particles compress and stretch in the same direction the sound is travelling, making areas of high pressure (compressions) and low pressure (rarefactions).
questions.source: CHS Y8 Science KM, Unit 3 Waves, Light and Sound

further_learning.title: Sound, Light and Vision – Oak National Academy

questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: How is sound produced?
questions.hint: Touch a speaker when music plays — what can you feel?
questions.explanation: Sound is made by vibrations. The vibrating object pushes air particles, and the pulses of pressure travel outwards as a sound wave.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Science KM, Unit 3 Waves, Light and Sound

further_learning.title: Sound, Light and Vision – Oak National Academy

questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: Sound cannot travel through which of these?
questions.hint: Sound needs particles to vibrate — what doesn't have any?
questions.explanation: Sound needs a medium (solid, liquid or gas) to travel because it relies on particles colliding. A vacuum has no particles, so no sound. That's why space is silent.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Science KM, Unit 3 Waves, Light and Sound

further_learning.title: Sound, Light and Vision – Oak National Academy

questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: Order these from SLOWEST to FASTEST speed of sound.
questions.hint: Closer-packed particles transfer vibrations faster.
questions.explanation: Sound travels fastest in solids (steel ~5000 m/s), slower in liquids (water ~1500 m/s), slowest in gases (air ~340 m/s). Tighter particle spacing = faster vibration transfer.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Science KM, Unit 3 Waves, Light and Sound

further_learning.title: Sound, Light and Vision – Oak National Academy

questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: Which property of a sound wave determines its pitch?
questions.hint: High pitch = lots of waves per second.
questions.explanation: Pitch depends on frequency. High frequency = high pitch (squeak). Low frequency = low pitch (rumble).
questions.source: CHS Y8 Science KM, Unit 3 Waves, Light and Sound

further_learning.title: Sound, Light and Vision – Oak National Academy

questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: Which property of a sound wave determines its loudness?
questions.hint: Bigger waves carry more energy → louder sound.
questions.explanation: Loudness depends on amplitude. Larger amplitude waves carry more energy, making louder sounds.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Science KM, Unit 3 Waves, Light and Sound

further_learning.title: Sound, Light and Vision – Oak National Academy

questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: What is the typical frequency range of human hearing?
questions.hint: 20 to 20 thousand.
questions.explanation: Humans hear from about 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz (20 kHz). This range narrows with age — older people lose the top end first.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Science KM, Unit 3 Waves, Light and Sound

further_learning.title: Sound, Light and Vision – Oak National Academy

questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: Sound waves above 20,000 Hz are called what?
questions.hint: 'Ultra' means above the human range.
questions.explanation: Ultrasound is above 20 kHz — too high for human ears. It's used in medical scanning, sonar and cleaning equipment. Infrasound is below 20 Hz.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Science KM, Unit 3 Waves, Light and Sound

further_learning.title: Sound, Light and Vision – Oak National Academy

questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: Order these parts of the ear in the order sound travels through them.
questions.hint: Sound enters the outer ear and ends up as a signal sent to the brain.
questions.explanation: Sound goes: ear canal → ear drum (vibrates) → ossicles (amplify) → cochlea (converts vibration to nerve signal) → auditory nerve → brain.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Science KM, Unit 3 Waves, Light and Sound

further_learning.title: Sound, Light and Vision – Oak National Academy

questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: You see lightning and hear thunder 6 seconds later. Sound travels at 340 m/s in air. How far away is the storm (in metres)?
questions.hint: distance = speed × time
questions.explanation: distance = speed × time = 340 × 6 = 2040 m. Light travels almost instantly, so the delay is just the sound time.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Science KM, Unit 3 Waves, Light and Sound

further_learning.title: Sound, Light and Vision – Oak National Academy

questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: What is an echo?
options: A sound that travels through walls
A sound that has been reflected back
questions.answer: A sound that has been reflected back
questions.hint: It happens when sound bounces off a surface.
questions.explanation: An echo is a sound wave reflected from a hard surface back to the listener. Soft surfaces absorb sound; hard flat surfaces reflect it well.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Science KM, Unit 3 Waves, Light and Sound

further_learning.title: Sound, Light and Vision – Oak National Academy

questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: A submarine sends an ultrasound pulse. It takes 0.4 s for the echo to return from the seabed. Sound travels at 1500 m/s in water. How deep is the seabed (in metres)?
questions.hint: Total distance = speed × time. But that's THERE AND BACK — depth is half.
questions.explanation: Total distance = 1500 × 0.4 = 600 m. Sound went down AND came back, so depth = 600 ÷ 2 = 300 m. This is how echo sounding (sonar) works.
questions.source: UK NC KS3

further_learning.title: Sound, Light and Vision – Oak National Academy

questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: What is the approximate speed of light in a vacuum (in m/s)? Give your answer as 300,000,000 or in standard form.
questions.hint: Three hundred million metres per second.
questions.explanation: Light in a vacuum travels at about 3 × 10⁸ m/s (300,000,000 m/s). Nothing can travel faster.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Science KM, Unit 3 Waves, Light and Sound

further_learning.title: Sound, Light and Vision – Oak National Academy

questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: Compared with sound, light travels...
questions.hint: You see the firework before you hear it.
questions.explanation: Light travels at 3 × 10⁸ m/s; sound in air about 340 m/s. Light is roughly a million times faster — which is why you see lightning before hearing thunder.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Science KM, Unit 3 Waves, Light and Sound

further_learning.title: Sound, Light and Vision – Oak National Academy

questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: Can light travel through a vacuum?
options: Yes — that's how sunlight reaches Earth
questions.answer: Yes — that's how sunlight reaches Earth
questions.hint: Light is an electromagnetic wave — different from sound.
questions.explanation: Unlike sound, light is an electromagnetic wave and doesn't need a medium. It travels through the vacuum of space, which is how the Sun's light reaches us.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Science KM, Unit 3 Waves, Light and Sound

further_learning.title: Sound, Light and Vision – Oak National Academy

questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: What is the law of reflection?
options: Angle of incidence is twice the angle of reflection
Angle of incidence equals angle of reflection
Reflection only happens at smooth surfaces
questions.answer: Angle of incidence equals angle of reflection
questions.hint: The angle going in matches the angle coming out.
questions.explanation: Law of reflection: angle of incidence = angle of reflection (both measured from the normal). The normal is a line perpendicular to the mirror surface.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Science KM, Unit 3 Waves, Light and Sound

further_learning.title: Sound, Light and Vision – Oak National Academy

questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: A ray of light hits a mirror at an angle of incidence of 35°. What is the angle of reflection?
questions.hint: Law of reflection.
questions.explanation: Angle of incidence = angle of reflection. 35° in → 35° out. Both measured from the normal.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Science KM, Unit 3 Waves, Light and Sound

further_learning.title: Sound, Light and Vision – Oak National Academy

questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: What is 'diffuse reflection'?
options: Reflection from a perfectly smooth surface
Reflection from a rough surface, scattering light in many directions
questions.answer: Reflection from a rough surface, scattering light in many directions
questions.hint: Why doesn't a wooden table act like a mirror?
questions.explanation: On smooth surfaces (mirrors) parallel rays stay parallel — specular reflection. On rough surfaces rays scatter in all directions — diffuse reflection. That's why most objects don't act like mirrors.
questions.source: UK NC KS3

further_learning.title: Sound, Light and Vision – Oak National Academy

questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: What is refraction?
options: Light bending as it passes from one material to another
questions.answer: Light bending as it passes from one material to another
questions.hint: Like when a straw looks bent in a glass of water.
questions.explanation: Refraction is the bending of light as it moves between materials with different densities (e.g. air to glass to water). It happens because light changes speed in different materials.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Science KM, Unit 3 Waves, Light and Sound

further_learning.title: Sound, Light and Vision – Oak National Academy

questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: When light travels from air into a denser material like glass, it bends...
questions.hint: Light slows down going into glass — that bends it towards the perpendicular.
questions.explanation: Going from less dense to more dense (air → glass), light slows and bends TOWARDS the normal. Going the other way (glass → air), it speeds up and bends AWAY from the normal.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Science KM, Unit 3 Waves, Light and Sound

further_learning.title: Sound, Light and Vision – Oak National Academy

questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: What happens when white light passes through a prism?
options: It splits into the colours of the spectrum
questions.answer: It splits into the colours of the spectrum
questions.hint: Think rainbow.
questions.explanation: A prism splits white light into a spectrum because each colour refracts by a different amount. Red bends least, violet bends most. This is called dispersion.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Science KM, Unit 3 Waves, Light and Sound

further_learning.title: Sound, Light and Vision – Oak National Academy

questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: Put the colours of the visible spectrum in order from LONGEST to SHORTEST wavelength.
questions.hint: Mnemonic: Richard Of York Gave Battle In Vain. Red has the longest wavelength.
questions.explanation: Visible spectrum from longest to shortest wavelength: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet. Red bends least in a prism; violet bends most.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Science KM, Unit 3 Waves, Light and Sound

further_learning.title: Sound, Light and Vision – Oak National Academy

questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: Why does a red apple look red?
options: It absorbs red light and reflects other colours
It reflects red light and absorbs the other colours
questions.answer: It reflects red light and absorbs the other colours
questions.hint: Coloured objects subtract colours from white light.
questions.explanation: An object's colour is the wavelength of light it REFLECTS. A red apple absorbs all other colours and reflects red. A white object reflects all colours; a black object absorbs them all.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Science KM, Unit 3 Waves, Light and Sound

further_learning.title: Sound, Light and Vision – Oak National Academy

questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: A blue book is viewed under a red light. What colour does it appear?
questions.hint: If only red light is present and the book absorbs red... what's reflected?
questions.explanation: The blue book reflects only blue light. Under red light there's no blue light to reflect, so the book absorbs all the red and appears black.
questions.source: UK NC KS3

further_learning.title: Sound, Light and Vision – Oak National Academy

questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: What does a green filter do to white light?
options: It reflects green and lets through everything else
It absorbs all colours except green
questions.answer: It absorbs all colours except green
questions.hint: Filters work by absorption — they let one colour through.
questions.explanation: A coloured filter transmits its own colour and absorbs the others. A green filter only lets green light through; the rest is absorbed.
questions.source: UK NC KS3

further_learning.title: Sound, Light and Vision – Oak National Academy

questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: Which part of the eye focuses light onto the retina?
questions.hint: It changes shape to focus on near or far objects.
questions.explanation: The lens fine-tunes the focus of light onto the retina. The cornea also refracts incoming light. The pupil controls how much light enters; the iris controls the pupil's size.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Science KM, Unit 3 Waves, Light and Sound

further_learning.title: Sound, Light and Vision – Oak National Academy

questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: What is the function of the retina?
options: Controls how much light enters the eye
Detects light and sends signals to the brain
Protects the front of the eye
questions.answer: Detects light and sends signals to the brain
questions.hint: It's at the back of the eye, full of light-sensitive cells.
questions.explanation: The retina contains rod cells (light/dark) and cone cells (colour). They convert light into electrical signals sent down the optic nerve to the brain.
questions.source: CHS Y8 Science KM, Unit 3 Waves, Light and Sound

further_learning.title: Sound, Light and Vision – Oak National Academy

questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: Order these parts of the electromagnetic spectrum from LONGEST to SHORTEST wavelength.
questions.hint: Mnemonic: 'Roman Men Invented Very Unusual X-ray Guns'.
questions.explanation: EM spectrum, longest to shortest wavelength: Radio, Microwave, Infrared, Visible, Ultraviolet, X-rays, Gamma. As wavelength decreases, frequency and energy both increase.
questions.source: UK NC KS3

further_learning.title: Sound, Light and Vision – Oak National Academy

questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: Which type of electromagnetic wave is used for communication, including mobile phones and Wi-Fi?
questions.hint: These travel long distances and pass through walls.
questions.explanation: Radio waves and microwaves are used for broadcasting, mobile signals, Wi-Fi and satellites. They can pass through walls and travel long distances.
questions.source: UK NC KS3

further_learning.title: Sound, Light and Vision – Oak National Academy

questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: Which EM wave is most useful for taking pictures of broken bones?
questions.hint: They pass through soft tissue but are absorbed by bone.
questions.explanation: X-rays pass through soft tissue but are absorbed by denser bone, so bones show up white on the photographic plate. Too much exposure damages cells, so doses are kept low.
questions.source: UK NC KS3

further_learning.title: Sound, Light and Vision – Oak National Academy

questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: Why is too much ultraviolet (UV) from the Sun dangerous?
options: It can damage skin cells and cause skin cancer
It only makes you tan, never burns
questions.answer: It can damage skin cells and cause skin cancer
questions.hint: Sunscreen protects against it — why?
questions.explanation: UV is high-energy enough to damage DNA in skin cells. Short-term effect: sunburn. Long-term: increased skin cancer risk and premature ageing. Sunscreen blocks UV.
questions.source: UK NC KS3

further_learning.title: Sound, Light and Vision – Oak National Academy

questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: Which EM wave is given off by hot objects and used in TV remotes and thermal imaging?
questions.hint: All warm objects emit it — the word means 'below red'.
questions.explanation: Infrared is emitted by anything warmer than its surroundings. Used in remote controls, thermal cameras and electric heaters. It's what you feel as radiated heat.
questions.source: UK NC KS3

further_learning.title: Sound, Light and Vision – Oak National Academy

questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: Select all the statements that are true about ALL electromagnetic waves.
options: They travel at the speed of light in a vacuum
They can be reflected and refracted
They all have the same wavelength
answer: They travel at the speed of light in a vacuum
They can be reflected and refracted
questions.hint: EM waves DON'T need particles. They have different wavelengths.
questions.explanation: All EM waves: travel at 3 × 10⁸ m/s in vacuum, are transverse, transfer energy, and can be reflected/refracted. They do NOT need particles (unlike sound) and have different wavelengths across the spectrum.
questions.source: UK NC KS3

further_learning.title: Sound, Light and Vision – Oak National Academy

questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: What type of wave is a sound wave?
questions.hint: Think about how a slinky spring moves when you push it back and forth.
questions.explanation: Sound waves are longitudinal — particles vibrate parallel to the direction the wave travels, creating compressions and rarefactions.
questions.source: UK NC KS3

further_learning.title: Sound, Light and Vision – Oak National Academy

questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: Light waves (and other electromagnetic waves) are which type of wave?
questions.hint: Think about a rope being shaken up and down — the oscillation is at right angles to the direction of travel.
questions.explanation: Light and all electromagnetic waves are transverse — the oscillations are perpendicular (at right angles) to the direction of energy travel.
questions.source: UK NC KS3

further_learning.title: Sound, Light and Vision – Oak National Academy

questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: In a transverse wave, how do particles move relative to the direction the wave travels?
options: Perpendicular (at right angles) to the wave direction
In circles around the wave direction
They do not move at all
questions.answer: Perpendicular (at right angles) to the wave direction
questions.hint: Transverse — like a rope being shaken side-to-side while the wave moves along the rope.
questions.explanation: In a transverse wave, particles oscillate at right angles to the direction of energy travel. Examples include light, water ripples and waves on a string.
questions.source: UK NC KS3

further_learning.title: Sound, Light and Vision – Oak National Academy

questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: In a longitudinal wave, how do particles move relative to the direction the wave travels?
questions.hint: Think about pushing a slinky spring back and forth along its length.
questions.explanation: In a longitudinal wave, particles vibrate back and forth along the same direction as the wave travels. Sound is the main example at KS3.
questions.source: UK NC KS3

further_learning.title: Sound, Light and Vision – Oak National Academy

questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: What is a 'compression' in a longitudinal wave?
options: A region where particles are spread far apart
A region where particles are pushed close together
The peak of a transverse wave
The trough of a transverse wave
questions.answer: A region where particles are pushed close together
questions.hint: Compress = squash together. Think of squashing a spring.
questions.explanation: A compression is a region of high pressure in a longitudinal wave where particles are crowded close together. In sound, compressions are areas of higher air pressure.
questions.source: UK NC KS3

further_learning.title: Sound, Light and Vision – Oak National Academy

questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: What is a 'rarefaction' in a longitudinal wave?
options: A region where particles are packed closely together
A region where particles are spread further apart
questions.answer: A region where particles are spread further apart
questions.hint: Rare = less common, spread out. The opposite of a compression.
questions.explanation: A rarefaction is a region of low pressure in a longitudinal wave where particles are spread further apart than normal. Rarefactions alternate with compressions as the wave travels.
questions.source: UK NC KS3

further_learning.title: Sound, Light and Vision – Oak National Academy

questions.subject: science
questions.prompt: Which of these are transverse waves? (Select all that apply)
questions.hint: Sound and seismic P-waves are longitudinal. EM waves and water ripples are transverse.
questions.explanation: Transverse waves oscillate perpendicular to their direction of travel. Light, water surface waves and radio waves are all transverse. Sound and seismic P-waves are longitudinal — particles vibrate parallel to the wave direction.
questions.source: UK NC KS3

further_learning.title: Sound, Light and Vision – Oak National Academy
